content: The National Health Workforce Accounts (NHWA) system is designed to provide comparable data for monitoring critical aspects of human resources for health (HRH) within healthcare systems. The data categories within this system are reflected in the indicators outlined by the NHWA. The European Union Joint Action on Health Workforce Planning and Forecasting, which includes various reports and analyses on HRH-related indicators, has also contributed to the development of the NHWA indicators. The NHWA is an ongoing and evolving process. It is subject to regular review and updates to align with advancements in measurement methodologies and the changing trends in HRH. The metadata sheets for the NHWA indicators, as detailed in Part II of the NHWA Handbook, provide definitions, explanations, and methodologies for calculating these indicators. These sheets also include key terms, external references, and relevant data sources to enhance understanding and ensure accurate reporting. The metadata sheets follow a standardized structure for each indicator, including the indicator number (linked to its module and subcategory), thematic dimension, abbreviated and full names, numerator and denominator (for numeric indicators), disaggregation factors (e.g., by sex, age, or facility type), and definitions with technical notes. For capability indicators, questions and answer options are provided. The glossary defines key terms, and data reporting frequency is specified (e.g., annually or every three years). Potential data sources at the national level are listed in order of relevance, and further information or related links are included for context. The NHWA system also provides examples of its application. For instance, it supports the self-sustainability of the health workforce, as advocated by the WHO Global Code of Practice on the International Recruitment of Health Personnel. This involves effective workforce planning, education, training, and retention strategies to reduce reliance on recruiting migrant health personnel. Self-sustainability is achieved when national production compensates for workforce losses and adapts to population needs, though it is influenced by internal and external labor market factors. Relevant NHWA modules for this include Module 1 (active health workforce stock), Module 2 (education and training), and Module 5 (health labor market flows). Another example is addressing geographical imbalances in the health workforce distribution, particularly in underserved rural and remote areas. Monitoring these imbalances helps evaluate the impact of social, financial, and organizational determinants on health worker decisions and supports the Global Strategy on Human Resources for Health 2030 milestone of reducing inequalities in access to health workers. Relevant modules include Module 1 (active health workforce stock) and Module 5 (health labor market flows). The NHWA also emphasizes the importance of health worker training performance. The national supply of new health workers is critical to the success of health policies. Monitoring the implementation of educational plans is essential, as outlined in the Global Strategy on Human Resources for Health. Milestones include establishing inclusive institutional mechanisms for intersectoral coordination, accreditation systems for training institutions, and improving course completion rates in medical, nursing, and allied health training programs. Relevant modules include Module 2 (education and training), Module 3 (education regulation and accreditation), and Module 4 (education finances). The NHWA system provides a comprehensive list of health-related occupations, primarily disaggregated by occupation, using the International Standard Classification of Occupations (ISCO-08) where possible. Core occupational groups and occupations are identified to ensure harmonized monitoring across countries. This list should be adapted to national priorities and includes detailed occupational titles and ISCO-08 codes for monitoring the health workforce. Accreditation processes, mechanisms, and standards are integral to ensuring the quality of health workforce education programs. These systems are based on standards, supported by legislative instruments, and are independent, transparent, and accountable. Accreditation evaluates the quality of institutions or programs and stimulates quality improvement. Admission processes for health workforce education programs assess whether applicants meet the minimum entry requirements, which vary by country and program.
